paragraphs.source_en: Stone cities are particularly abundant in the central-southern part of the Tassili Plateau, called Tassili de Tamrit, where the majority of paintings are concentrated. In the northern part of the Tassili, stone cities are rare and the landscape is dominated by large plains. Besides the Algerian Tadrart and Acacus, painted shelters in wadies also exist in the Tassili, especially in its northwestern part where paintings are rare.

paragraphs.source_en: The difference in the landscape morphology between the Tassili, the Algerian Tadrart and the Acacus has affected the distribution of the paintings. Whereas in the Tassili there are abundant stone cities with a large number of shelters that were suitable for painting, in the Acacus and in the Algerian Tadrart shelters are rare and they are scattered over a vast area. On the Tassili Plateau the prehistoric painters could have chosen between many sites and rock walls for their image-making, but in the Tadrart and Acacus they had virtually no choice and they had to use any available wall. Since the paintings are most numerous on the Tassili Plateau where the suitable shelters are also most numerous, it is evident that the quantity of the paintings is related to the quantity of available rock walls.

paragraphs.source_en: A site may be visible from a very distant point, up to several dozens of kilometres away, which is mainly the case when a site is located on a hill (Fig. 3-9). Also sites in lowlands may be visible from faraway if situated in a large open plain. However, sites in lowlands are mostly hidden by other rock formations or small hills, so that they are not visible unless from a very short distance.

paragraphs.source_en: A large number of stone cities are crossed by one or more wadies, meaning that in prehistoric times they were crossed by rivers or streams therefore being directly connected to water courses. Paintings are placed inside stone cities or located near, and facing, the ancient river. Wadies in the Tassili, Algerian Tadrart and Acacus usually connect several sites; therefore the river may have been one of the main routes of communication between the sites.
